messages.subject: stan really works (or seems to)
parts:
Hi, Phil. I'm sharing this with the stan-dev list because I think they'll be happy to hear this too! Also they will have intuition about the speed. How long did your model take to run per effective sample size?
See you
A

On Jan 17, 2013, at 12:08 PM, Phillip Price wrote:

>
> On Jan 17, 2013, at 8:17 AM, Andrew Gelman wrote:
>
>> . . . remind me to tell you the story of the kosher restaurant. It's not an amazing story but it has a small twist with statistical content!
>
> Good. Let's speak soon.
>
> I'm using Stan! Perhaps this means I should have been using BUGS all along, but the last time I tried to use it for one of my current problems, a few years ago, it was just so slow that I gave up. The problem isn't how long it takes to run once I have a model --- if I had a good model I could tolerate taking four or five days for it to run--- it's that the development cycle was so long. I would work with a much smaller dataset than I really wanted to use, to try to speed things up, and then I would add something to the model and test it, and it would be slow even on the small dataset... I couldn't test more than one change per two days or something. Eventually I concluded that the vastly more complicated models that I really wanted to fit were simply untenable.
>
> But with Stan it's going great, to the point that I keep wondering if I'm somehow missing something and the results aren't as good as I think they are. Basically I am trying to fit a model that captures most of what I know about my problem. This results in a model with considerably more parameters than data points (of the order of 7000 of each), but with pretty tight constraints on the parameters or on combinations of them, through a moderately complicated model structure. I knew it would be possible in principle to fit this but I thought that in practice it might require a too delicate balance of distributional assumptions and prior estimates: I thought I'd end up overfitting, or underfitting, or something. But no, so far so good. It is such a big change in the models I am trying to fit that it seems qualitative rather than just quantitative, the way going from Conestoga wagons to jet airplanes isn't just a quantitatively faster way to cross the country.
>
> So: good job!
>
> P
>
